name: Guru Nanak
info: Guru Nanak was an Indian spiritual teacher, mystic and poet of Punjab, born in 1469, regarded as the founder of Sikhism and the first of its ten gurus, who taught devotion to one God and the equality of all people.

facts.born: 15 April 1469, at Rāi Bhoi Dī Talvaṇḍī (now Nankana Sahib, Punjab, Pakistan), a Bedi Khatri; another tradition gives the month of Kārtik (November)
facts.died: 22 September 1539, at Kartarpur, aged 70, after naming Bhai Lehna (Guru Angad) as his successor
facts.role: First of the ten Sikh gurus; Sikhs regard him as the founder of their faith, and scholars describe him as a poet and teacher in the nirguni tradition of the Bhakti movement
facts.known: Teaching Ik Onkar, one God; the Japji Sahib; 974 hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib; the udasis; the settlement at Kartarpur; langar; naam japo, kirat karo and vand chhako

t: Nanak was born into a Hindu Khatri family in Punjab, worked in the state stores at Sultanpur, and, according to Sikh belief, received a divine call in about 1496 after vanishing into the Bein river.
He taught one God, Ik Onkar, the equality of people regardless of gender, caste or religion, and a householder's life of honest work, sharing and remembrance of the divine name.
He settled at Kartarpur, where his community practised communal eating and singing, and he passed the guruship to Bhai Lehna, who became Guru Angad, not to his sons.
dyk: Guru Arjan included 974 hymns by Nanak in the Ādi Granth in 1604, and the Japji forms the opening of the work.
ev: Nanak is born at Rāi Bhoi Dī Talvaṇḍī, now Nankana Sahib
He disappears into the Bein river and returns after three or four days, saying that there is no Hindu and no Muslim
He visits the Sylhet region in Bengal, according to modern accounts
Around the age of 55 he settles at Kartarpur on the Ravi, where the Nanak Panth takes shape
He names Bhai Lehna as Guru Angad and dies at Kartarpur on 22 September
Guru Arjan includes 974 of his hymns in the Ādi Granth

sections.early:
Nanak was born on 15 April 1469 at Rāi Bhoi Dī Talvaṇḍī, now Nankana Sahib in Punjab, Pakistan, then part of the Lahore province of the Delhi Sultanate. He was a Bedi Khatri. A second tradition places his birth in November, in the month of Kārtik, and the question is still debated: most janamsakhis, the traditional biographies, say Baisakh, and the festival was held in April as late as 1815.

His father, Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, called Mehta Kalu, was the village patwari, an accountant of crop revenue, who worked for Rai Bullar, a Bhatti Rajput who had converted to Islam. His mother was Tripta, and his elder sister Nanaki was four or five years older. His childhood friend Mardana was a Muslim rababi.

According to the janamsakhis, he studied accounting and the Devanagari script, then the Vedas, and at nine went to a maktab to learn Persian and Arabic. His father hoped he would take up accounting or trade, but he spent time with sadhus and sufis. Sikh lore says he refused the janaeu thread at his initiation, which began his break with orthodox traditions. Sources that were written to honour him include many miracles, such as a shadow from a tree or a cobra shading his sleeping head. Scholars treat these as hagiography.
sections.rise:
Nanak married Sulakhani, daughter of Mūl Chand, on 24 September 1487 at Batala. They had two sons, Sri Chand, born in 1494, and Lakhmi Chand, born in 1496 or 1497. Through his sister's husband, Jai Ram, he found work at the modikhana, a store for revenues, in the service of Daulat Khan, the Lahore governor, at Sultanpur. He worked there as custodian of the stores for about twelve years, singing hymns with Mardana at dawn and night. Scholars note that his hymns' references to government probably come from this period.

According to Sikh belief, he disappeared while bathing in the Bein river. His clothes were found, and people assumed he had drowned. He returned on the third or fourth day, silent, and then said: 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.' The Janamsakhi literature says that during his absence he was brought to the court of God, was given amrit and a robe of honour, and was told to spread naam simran, dan, isnan and seva. His reply to the test of how to praise the divine name was the opening of the Japji. Sikhs date this event to about the age of 33, while Kapur Singh dates it to about 1496, when he was 27. The first to accept that he had reached enlightenment was his sister Nanaki.
sections.deeds:
After the event at Sultanpur he left government service and began a spiritual journey. The Janamsakhis describe lengthy tours, the udasis, across the Indian subcontinent and beyond, usually four: east to Varanasi, Bodh Gaya, Bengal and Assam; south to Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka; north to Ladakh and Tibet; and west to Mecca, Medina and Baghdad. Mardana accompanied him on the eastern and western tours. He wore clothing associated with both fakirs and sadhus, held discourses with Hindu and Muslim figures, and visited temples, mosques and Sufi centres. He is said to have witnessed Babur's invasion at Saidpur, which four hymns, the Babur Vani, record.

At about fifty he gathered a following, the Nanak Panth, and at about fifty-five he settled at Kartarpur, on land a follower donated beside the Ravi. He lived as a householder and taught honest work, devotion and sharing. The community practised communal eating, langar, selfless service, and singing together at dawn. He taught the equality of humankind, rejected the divisions of varna, said that women were not impure or inferior, and criticised the rulers of his day for greed and cruelty. The Japji was finalised there and put into the daily recitation.
sections.opponents:
The sources record resistance and disagreement more than organised persecution. Nanak's father is said to have struck him for spending money on feeding hungry sadhus, and his family thought his withdrawal showed a lack of ambition and, at one point, possession. After his saying that there was no Hindu and no Muslim, a Qazi complained to Daulat Khan Lodhi, and Nanak was summoned to Sultanpur.

The Sikh tradition holds that his rejection of rites such as the janaeu thread began his break with Vedic and Hindu orthodoxy, and he denied the caste divisions of varna. He also criticised the prevailing political regimes for greed and cruelty.

Modern scholarship disputes much of the life. The janamsakhis, the Bala, Miharban, Adi and Puratan traditions, were written by later followers with no intention of exact history, and Callewaert and Snell find that early Sikh texts do not hold the travel stories. The Baghdad stone with an inscription in a Turkish script is read as 1511 to 1512 by some and as 1521 to 1522 by others, and Western scholars argue that it is from the 19th century. No Middle Eastern record mentions a visit. The Bala janamsakhi's October birth date was written by the Handalis, a sect that wished to depict its own founder as superior to Nanak.
sections.last:
Nanak examined his sons and, according to Bhai Gurdas, both failed. Sri Chand was an ascetic, a lifestyle Nanak had reprimanded, and Lakhmi Das was not interested in religion. Nanak appointed Bhai Lehna of Khadur as his successor and renamed him Guru Angad, 'one's very own'. Lehna had been a worshipper of Durga. The ceremony placed a coconut and five paisse before him, with Nanak bowing toward him. Sikhs hold that the guruship passed from Nanak to Angad as one light passing between two bodies. Mandair says that by choosing a successor Nanak meant his work to continue, which helped the early community survive as a distinct group.

Nanak died on 22 September 1539 at Kartarpur, at the age of 70. According to the Puratan Janamsakhi, his Muslim and Hindu followers quarrelled over what to do with his body. When they pulled at the sheet covering him, they found only flowers. The Muslims and Hindus each took flowers and buried or cremated them by their own customs. Scholars note that such stories resemble miracle stories told of Sufi pirs.

After his death Guru Angad moved the community to Khadur, as Nanak's sons claimed the property at Kartarpur. The Ravi later washed away his mausoleum, and his son reburied the urn with his ashes on the left bank, where Dera Baba Nanak grew up.
sections.legacy:
Sikhs regard Nanak as the founder of Sikhism and the first of ten gurus, and hold that his sanctity and authority passed to each of the nine who followed. His 974 hymns stand in the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs revere as the final and perpetual guru. They include the Japji Sahib, the Asa di Var and the Sidh Gosht. He wrote in a composite vernacular, Sant Bhasha, in simple metre and with comparisons, and he called himself a poet. His birthday is celebrated as Guru Nanak Gurpurab, held on the full moon of Kārtik since at least 1868.

Sikhs understand his teaching as naam japo, kirat karo and vand chhako, which are remembering God's name, honest work and sharing. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh sees the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 as an attempt to return to the equality of Kartarpur.

Scholars disagree about what produced his teaching. Earlier writers called it a mixture of Hinduism and Islam. Recent work sets it among the nirguni Sant and Bhakti movements, with some Islamic influence, and James R. Lewis criticises the label 'syncretic'. Sikhs differ on whether he was a guru and not a prophet, or an incarnation of God.

Other traditions claim him: the Bahá'í Faith calls him a saint of the highest order, many Hindus follow Nanakpanthi teachings, the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community holds that he was a Muslim saint, and many Tibetans have regarded him as an incarnation of Padmasambhava.

summary: Guru Nanak, born in 1469 in Punjab, taught devotion to one God and the equality of people, composed 974 hymns kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, and founded a community at Kartarpur. Sikhs regard him as the first of their ten gurus.
references: Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs (Oxford University Press, 2004)
William Owen Cole, The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices (Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1978)
Louise E. Fenech, The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Hari Ram Gupta, History of the Sikhs: The Sikh Gurus, 1469-1708 (Munshiram Manoharlal, 1984)
notes: Birth: 15 April 1469 as the article's lede gives it; the Kattak (November) tradition is stated in facts and early.
Age at the revelation: the article gives 33 (Sikh belief) and 27 (Kapur Singh, c. 1496); I kept both and set the event as 'c. 1496'.

'1520s' for Kartarpur: the article says around age 55 (about 1524) and that the Global Institute of Sikh Studies puts the start of the religion at c. 1520; check that '1520s' is acceptable or change to 'c. 1520'.
